Lucas Cho Ayaba looks on during the trial at the District Court in Oslo, November 24, 2026. [Stian Lysberg Solum/EPA]By Al Jazeera Staff and AFPPublished On 24 Nov 202624 Nov 2026
Cameroonian separatist leader Lucas Cho Ayaba has pleaded not guilty in a Norwegian court to being an accessory to war crimes and “terrorism”, charges that carry a sentence of up to 30 years.
The 54-year-old, who appeared in a court in Oslo on Tuesday, is accused of involvement in planning two attacks in Cameroon from Norway, helping to select targets and pay for explosives.

Prosecutors say Ayaba, also known as Cho Lucas Yabah, remotely led the separatist Amazonia Governing Council and commanded its armed wing, the Amazonia Defence Forces, from 2017 until 2024, when he was arrested in Norway, where he has lived since 2008.
Francophone-majority Cameroon has been gripped for nearly 10 years by conflict between state security forces and separatists demanding the independence of two Anglophone regions in the country’s west to form what supporters call “Ambazonia”.
In February 2023, three improvised devices exploded during a mountain run race near Buea in southwestern Cameroon, killing a 38-year-old woman and injuring 19 civilians.

Supporters of Lebanese Shia movement Hezbollah hold up portraits of slain leader Hassan Nasrallah as they wave flags of the group during a ceremony held to mark the second anniversary of Nasrallah's killing in a strike by Israel, in Beirut's southern suburbs on September 27, 2026 [File: AFP]By Justin SalhaniPublished On 24 Nov 202624 Nov 2026
Beirut, Lebanon – New United States sanctions on an organisation linked to the Iranian-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah will have a limited impact beyond the political messaging the punishment provides, analysts have told Al Jazeera.
The organisation – a charity called Wa Ta’awanu Association – was among the entities and individuals targeted by the US Treasury in new sanctions announced on November 18, accusing it of being a “front organisation” for Hezbollah. The Treasury said the sanctions were an effort to disrupt Hezbollah’s financing networks.

But experts told Al Jazeera, the sanctions will do little to change Lebanon’s domestic situation, in which Hezbollah has been one of the major powers – if not the major power – over the past two decades.

Soufiane Rahimi, right, celebrates scoring Morocco's third goal against Canada in the last 16 of the World Cup with Achraf Hakimi [Hannah Mckay/Reuters]By Doyinsola IbidunniPublished On 24 Nov 202624 Nov 2026
Morocco’s growing influence in African football is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.
From reaching the semifinals of the 2022 FIFA World Cup to hosting major continental competitions and preparing to cohost the 2030 World Cup, it has arguably become Africa’s dominant footballing nation.
Morocco is also preparing to welcome FIFA’s 77th Congress in Rabat on March 18, 2027, and the country hosted the last two editions of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) Awards. Three of its players – Achraf Hakimi, Brahim Diaz and Ismael Saibari – feature on the 10-person shortlist for the 2026 men’s CAF Player of the Year award.
For some, Morocco represents what sustained investment, strategic planning and football diplomacy can achieve. Others, however, question whether its growing concentration of hosting opportunities and institutional influence is creating an imbalance within African football.
Kamilla Swart, an associate professor and Director of the Master of Science in Sport and Entertainment Management programme at Hamad Bin Khalifa University in Doha, Qatar, says Morocco’s current position is the product of a strategy developed over several years.
“I think it’s a case of Morocco building its expertise over a long period of time,” she said.
“So if you even think of, you know, everybody talks about the Mohammed VI Football Academy that was inaugurated in 2010. So it’s not something that’s just happened now.”
